title: Idioms and Fixed Expressions
description: Understand and use common idioms for work, relationships and decisions; master binomials such as pros and cons and by and large; and learn which fixed expressions suit formal and informal registers.

lessons.title: Back to the Drawing Board: Idioms for Work
lessons.summary: Understand and use idioms that describe starting, planning, effort and progress at work.
objectives: Understand idioms such as get the ball rolling, cut corners and pull your weight
Use work idioms naturally in meetings and informal emails
Recognise that idioms have a fixed form
lessons.completionCriteria: Read all sections and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### What is an idiom?
An **idiom** is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words. 'Back to the drawing board' has nothing to do with drawing; it means 'we must start planning again because the previous plan failed'. Idioms are extremely common in spoken English, in workplace conversation, in journalism and in fiction. At C1, you are expected to **understand** a wide range of idioms and **use** a selection of them accurately and appropriately.

### Idioms for work and projects
| Idiom | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| get the ball rolling | start an activity | Let's get the ball rolling with a quick round of introductions. |
| back to the drawing board | start again after a failure | The client rejected the design, so it's back to the drawing board. |
| cut corners | do something cheaply or carelessly to save time or money | We can't afford to cut corners on safety. |
| pull your weight | do your fair share of the work | Everyone needs to pull their weight. |
| call it a day | stop working for now | We've done enough; let's call it a day. |
| on the same page | in agreement; understanding the situation in the same way | Let's make sure we're all on the same page. |
| think outside the box | think creatively | We need to think outside the box to cut costs. |
| a steep learning curve | a situation where you must learn a lot quickly | Joining a tech start-up was a steep learning curve. |
| up in the air | undecided | The launch date is still up in the air. |
| touch base | make brief contact | I'll touch base with you on Friday. |

### Fixed form, flexible grammar
You can change the **grammar** of an idiom (tense, pronouns) but not its **key words**:
- Correct: 'She **cut corners**.' / 'They **have been cutting corners**.' / 'Everyone **pulled their weight**.'
- Wrong: '*cut edges*', '*pull your weight up*', '*on the same paper*'.

Changing one word usually makes the idiom sound wrong or even meaningless to native speakers.

### Using idioms well
1. **Context**: work idioms are common in meetings, informal emails and conversations with colleagues, but they are usually avoided in formal reports and academic essays.
2. **Frequency**: use them occasionally. A sentence full of idioms sounds unnatural ('Let's get the ball rolling and think outside the box so we're on the same page').
3. **Audience**: international colleagues may not know every idiom, so clarity sometimes matters more than colour.

### Learning strategy
Learn idioms in **full example sentences** and group them by topic or by image (ball, corner, box). Note whether each idiom is positive, negative or neutral; 'cut corners', for example, is always critical.

### Indonesian note
Some idioms have Indonesian parallels: *kembali ke titik nol* (back to square one / back to the drawing board), *setengah hati* (half-hearted). Others have no direct equivalent and must be learned as whole units.

lessons.title: See Eye to Eye: Idioms for Relationships
lessons.summary: Describe friendships, disagreements and reconciliation with common idioms.
objectives: Understand idioms such as hit it off, see eye to eye and bury the hatchet
Describe conflict and reconciliation idiomatically
Use relationship idioms with correct grammar
lessons.completionCriteria: Read all sections and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Talking about relationships
Relationships, both personal and professional, are one of the richest areas of idiomatic English. These idioms appear constantly in conversation, TV series, novels and magazine articles.

### Positive relationships
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| hit it off (with someone) | like each other immediately |
| get on like a house on fire | have a very friendly relationship |
| see eye to eye (with someone) | agree |
| break the ice | make people feel relaxed when they first meet |
| on the same wavelength | thinking in a similar way |

### Problems and conflict
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| rub someone up the wrong way | annoy someone (often without meaning to) |
| give someone the cold shoulder | deliberately ignore someone |
| at loggerheads (with someone) | in strong disagreement |
| on the rocks | (of a relationship) having serious problems |
| fall out (with someone) | stop being friends after an argument |

### Reconciliation
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| bury the hatchet | end a disagreement and become friends again |
| clear the air | discuss a problem openly to remove tension |
| make up (with someone) | become friends again after an argument |

### Grammar notes
- *Hit it off* uses the fixed object *it*: 'Rina and Sari **hit it off** immediately.' (past: *hit*)
- *See eye to eye* is mostly used in the **negative**: 'My manager and I **don't always see eye to eye**.'
- *Get on like a house on fire* uses *get on* (British) or *get along* (American) — but the idiom itself is fixed with *get on*.
- *Fall out* and *make up* are phrasal verbs that also function like idioms: '**They fell out** over money but **made up** a week later.'

### Register and tone
Most relationship idioms are neutral to informal. In a workplace email, 'We don't always see eye to eye, but we work well together' is perfectly natural. In a formal report you would write 'There are occasional differences of opinion'.

### Indonesian note
Compare *akur* (get on well / see eye to eye), *bermusuhan* (be at loggerheads), *berbaikan* (make up / bury the hatchet), *mencairkan suasana* (break the ice). The last one is a close parallel: both languages use the image of ice or something frozen.

lessons.title: Take the Plunge: Idioms for Decisions
lessons.summary: Talk about hesitation, risk and decision-making with idioms such as sit on the fence, sleep on it and the ball is in your court.
objectives: Understand idioms for hesitating and deciding
Use idioms for risk and timing such as take the plunge and jump the gun
Respond naturally in discussions using decision idioms
lessons.completionCriteria: Read all sections and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Deciding and not deciding
Making decisions involves hesitation, risk, timing and responsibility. English has a large set of idioms for each stage.

### Hesitating
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| sit on the fence | avoid choosing a side |
| be in two minds (about something) | be unable to decide |
| have second thoughts | begin to doubt a decision already made |
| sleep on it | wait until the next day before deciding |
| weigh up the pros and cons | consider advantages and disadvantages |

### Taking action and risks
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| take the plunge | finally do something risky or important |
| jump the gun | act too soon, before the right time |
| a tough call | a difficult decision |
| play it safe | avoid risks |
| bite the bullet | accept something unpleasant because it is necessary |

### Responsibility and future decisions
| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| the ball is in your court | it is your turn to act or decide |
| cross that bridge when we come to it | deal with a problem only when it actually happens |
| go back on your word | break a promise |
| call the shots | be the person who makes the decisions |

### Using them in discussion
Decision idioms are very useful in meetings and negotiations:
- 'I'm **in two minds** about the proposal. Can I **sleep on it**?'
- 'We've made our offer. **The ball is in your court** now.'
- 'What if the supplier fails?' — '**Let's cross that bridge when we come to it.**'

They allow you to express a position politely and briefly.

### Watch the details
- *Sleep **on** it* (not *over* it).
- *Sit on the **fence*** (not *wall*).
- *Take the **plunge*** (not *dive*).
- *Burn your bridges* is a different idiom: it means to destroy any chance of returning to a previous situation.

### Indonesian note
*Plin-plan* or *ragu-ragu* relates to *be in two minds* / *sit on the fence*; *nekat* or *memberanikan diri* relates to *take the plunge*; *ingkar janji* = *go back on your word*; *gegabah / terburu-buru* = *jump the gun*.

lessons.title: Pros and Cons, By and Large: Binomials
lessons.summary: Use binomials (pairs of words joined by and/or) in their fixed order and understand their meanings.
objectives: Recognise common binomials such as pros and cons and by and large
Use binomials in their fixed, irreversible order
Understand the meaning of binomials in context
lessons.completionCriteria: Read all sections and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### What are binomials?
**Binomials** are fixed pairs of words joined by a conjunction, usually *and* or *or*: *pros and cons*, *sooner or later*, *by and large*. They are frequent in both speech and writing, and many are neutral enough for formal texts.

### Fixed order
The most important rule is that the **order is fixed**. Native speakers say *pros and cons*, never *cons and pros*; *safe and sound*, never *sound and safe*. Reversing the order sounds immediately wrong.

### Common binomials
| Binomial | Meaning |
|---|---|
| pros and cons | advantages and disadvantages |
| by and large | generally, on the whole |
| sooner or later | eventually |
| ups and downs | good and bad periods |
| odds and ends | small miscellaneous items |
| peace and quiet | calm, absence of noise |
| rules and regulations | official rules |
| give and take | willingness to compromise |
| safe and sound | unharmed |
| trial and error | testing different methods until one works |
| now and then | occasionally |
| first and foremost | most importantly |
| black and white | (in black and white) clearly written; (black-and-white) simple and clear-cut |
| touch and go | uncertain, risky |
| short and sweet | brief and pleasant |

### Patterns
Many binomials follow sound patterns that make them memorable:
- **alliteration** (same first sound): *part and parcel*, *safe and sound*
- **rhyme**: *wear and tear*, *high and dry*
- **repetition**: *again and again*, *on and on*, *round and round*
- **opposites**: *ups and downs*, *give and take*, *black and white*

The shorter word often comes first (*now and then*, *safe and sound*), but this is a tendency, not a rule. Learn each pair as one unit.

### Register
Some binomials are fine in academic writing: *by and large*, *first and foremost*, *trial and error*, *rules and regulations*, *pros and cons* (or *advantages and disadvantages* in very formal texts). Others are informal: *odds and ends*, *touch and go*, *short and sweet*.

### Indonesian note
Indonesian also has fixed pairs (*suka duka* = ups and downs, *untung rugi* = pros and cons, *lambat laun* = sooner or later, *pulang pergi* = there and back). Interestingly, the order of the Indonesian and English pairs does not always match, so learn each one separately.

lessons.title: Fixed Phrases and Register
lessons.summary: Choose fixed expressions that suit the situation: formal phrases for reports and letters, idioms for conversation, and avoid idioms in academic writing.
objectives: Use formal fixed phrases such as with regard to, in light of and on behalf of
Recognise informal idioms that are inappropriate in academic writing
Use idioms in their exact fixed form
lessons.completionCriteria: Read all sections and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Not all fixed phrases are idioms
Fixed expressions range from colourful idioms (*a piece of cake*) to neutral collocations (*make a decision*) and formal prepositional phrases (*with regard to*). An advanced speaker knows **which expressions belong in which context**.

### Formal fixed phrases
These are typical of reports, formal letters and academic writing:

| Formal phrase | Neutral meaning |
|---|---|
| with regard to / with respect to | about |
| in light of | considering, because of |
| on behalf of | for, representing |
| take into account / take into consideration | consider |
| in the vicinity of | near |
| in accordance with | following (rules) |
| on the grounds that | because |
| by virtue of | because of (formal) |
| in terms of | regarding a particular aspect |

### Informal idioms
These are natural in conversation and informal writing but **inappropriate** in academic essays and formal reports: *a piece of cake* (very easy), *at the end of the day* (ultimately), *no big deal* (not important), *over the moon* (very happy), *beat around the bush* (avoid saying something directly), *let the cat out of the bag* (reveal a secret), *raining cats and dogs* (raining heavily).

### Choosing the right register
| Informal | Neutral / formal |
|---|---|
| At the end of the day, the plan failed. | Ultimately, the plan failed. |
| The test was a piece of cake. | The test was straightforward. |
| It's no big deal. | It is of minor importance. |
| Let's not beat around the bush. | To be direct, ... |

### Fixed means fixed
Idioms and fixed phrases allow grammatical changes (tense, person), but **not** word substitutions:
- 'He **let the cat out of the bag**.' (not *from the bag*)
- 'It was **a piece of cake**.' (not *a slice of cake*)
- '**In light of** the evidence' (also *in the light of* in British English), but not *in the lights of*.

### Idioms in spoken presentations
In presentations, a few idioms can make you sound natural and engaging, especially with an informal audience. In academic conferences, prefer clear neutral expressions. Always consider whether your audience will understand the idiom.

### Indonesian note
Indonesian also distinguishes *bahasa baku* (formal, e.g. *sehubungan dengan* = with regard to, *atas nama* = on behalf of, *mengingat* = in light of) from colloquial expressions (*gampang banget* = a piece of cake). Applying the same sensitivity to English register is a key C1 skill.

mistakes.wrong: Learning to cook was a slice of cake for her.
mistakes.right: Learning to cook was a piece of cake for her.
mistakes.why: The fixed idiom is 'a piece of cake'.

mistakes.wrong: At the end of the day, the data support the hypothesis. (academic essay)
mistakes.right: Ultimately, the data support the hypothesis.
mistakes.why: 'At the end of the day' is too informal for academic writing.
The fixed phrase is 'with regard to' (or 'in regard to').

sections.summary: Fixed expressions range from formal phrases (with regard to, in light of, on behalf of, take into account) to informal idioms (a piece of cake, at the end of the day, no big deal). Match the expression to the register, and keep the words of idioms exactly as they are.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most suitable for a formal report?
options: In light of these findings, the committee recommends further research.
At the end of the day, the committee reckons we need more research.
It's no big deal, but the committee wants more research.
More research is a piece of cake for the committee.
questions.explanation: 'In light of' is a formal fixed phrase. The other options use informal idioms that are inappropriate in a report.

questions.prompt: Match each formal phrase with its neutral meaning.
questions.explanation: Formal fixed phrases often have simple neutral equivalents.

questions.prompt: This sentence is from an academic article. Find the part that is too informal.
segments: were, at the end of the day,
questions.explanation: 'At the end of the day' is a conversational idiom. In academic writing, use 'ultimately' or 'overall'.

questions.prompt: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.
segments: after years of watching her mother.
questions.explanation: The fixed idiom meaning 'very easy' is 'a piece of cake'.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the sentences in which the idiom is used in its correct fixed form.

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriate in an academic essay?

The findings were a piece of cake to interpret.
At the end of the day, the findings kind of support the hypothesis.
The findings hit the nail on the head, big time.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: 'By and large' is a neutral binomial acceptable in academic writing. The other options are informal.
